Reffy
28 Jan, 2025 @ 4:23pm 
Originally posted by Nil:
Took a year break, a lot of stuff and progression made no sense like you could constantly disassemble the same item, encounters were derpy and so on. The ability system was also terrible.

We went from bad to mediocre.
Sapphire subscription is fast, but still repetitive and too dumb.

The images use Wombo Art, which is heavily censored. Though it does a fine job creating generic images, such as buildings streets etc.

This game doesn't have world info, which is painful. You have to hope the AI knows about your setting, and you can't create your own besides the brief promt in the beginning.

The RPG system is barebones. Instead of using a simple system, it constantly creates new skills and then uses vague rolls that mostly seem to result in a minor failure.
I lost fights, items and NPC's because the AI decides I needed a "Alien Lore" skill to throw a grenade. Use any Tabletop RPG system. Not whatever this is.

You can't disable the main quest. Which is annoying, because the main quest is usually dumb and not what I want to do at all. Why can't I accept a main quest whenever I want?

Messages are terrible. The AI always tries to write stories instead of being a "Dungeon Master." This is nice if I want to read stories. But not when I want to play a game. The main selling point of this game was that compared to AI Dungeon, this is an actual game instead of just text. But when I play this "game", I get long replies where my character does things I don't want. NPC's and enemies that bump in, even though I'm nowhere near them.


IN SHORT; We went from a 2/10 to a 5/10.

Catzilla01
29 Jan, 2025 @ 12:10am 
Funny thing is that Ai Dungeon has been working on their own RPG mode called Heroes. So far the closed alpha seems to have more fleshed out systems and mechanics. It is being designed with an emergent narrative in mind. It does have a pretty in depth world creation, but testers have noted that it does take effort to create a world since it's not just a simple prompt. Some elements of world creation might get streamlined when it's closer to release. Quote from dev log: "And that’s the fascinating thing about all this: no one could have anticipated any of it, because it actually wasn’t scripted in any way. Instead, it’s what we call an emergent narrative: a story that arises spontaneously from interplay between the game’s various narrative systems—and the player. These systems work together to create an environment where compelling stories are bound to emerge, whatever the player decides to do. Since they don’t rely on artificial quest structures or forced plotting, the stories they drive feel natural in a way that most interactive fiction doesn’t. The result is total freedom for players to be and do whatever they want—while still experiencing a narrative that seems like it was written just for them.

"I could see myself playing this character alone for thousands of actions," another player noted after testing these changes. "There's no grand plot I'm supposed to follow. I'm just a character in a harsh world who has to make my own way in it, try to survive and make something of it. I'm not a hero unless I make myself one."

That's exactly what we're aiming for. Not a guided tour through a carefully curated adventure, but an open-ended struggle where your choices–and their consequences–actually matter.

This philosophy–that meaningful stories require real choices and genuine conflict–drove both our Wayfarer development and our Heroes redesign. By training our AI on carefully created data rich in adversity, loss, and consequence, we've created something that better understands the essential role of conflict in narrative. Not gratuitous violence or meaningless death, but the kind of genuine stakes that make victory taste sweeter and defeat sting deeper." The latest dev log talks more about the work they did to improve the engine: blog.latitude.io/heroes-dev-logs/16
